newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cigar smoking up, even among teen-agers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cigar smoking up, even among teen-agers.

text.p: Federal health officials said on Thursday that cigar smoking had increased among adults and that teenagers had joined the fad despite clear evidence that it posed a significant health risk.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said that almost 4.5 billion cigars were smoked in the United States last year. Consumption of larger cigars rose by 44.5 percent between 1993 and 1996, to approximately 3.09 billion cigars.
"There is a cigar fad in this country. We see cigars glamorized on TV, in movies and in magazines," Michael Eriksen, director of the CDC's Office on Smoking and Health, said.
A survey of more than 16,000 high school students last year found that 26.7 percent of them had smoked at least one cigar in the past year.
"This is the first report that has ever looked at cigar smoking among teenagers and we are shocked by the results," Eriksen said.

A study in two counties in New York state found 13 to 15 percent of ninth-grade students had smoked cigars in the past 30 days. In Massachusetts, a survey found that 14.5 percent of students in grades 9 through 12 had smoked at least one cigar in the past month.

The CDC said young people in New York found it easy to purchase cigars. "You would think that buying a cigar would be a more obvious inappropriate behaviour in a convenience store or a retail outlet, but we're finding even higher rates of illegal sales of cigars than we do with cigarettes," Eriksen said.
The health agency said cigar smoking can cause cancers of the oral cavity, larynx, oesophagus and lungs as well as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

"They can cause cancer and they can lead to nicotine addiction, just like other tobacco products," Eriksen said. "A typical cigar can be equivalent to an entire pack of cigarettes in terms of tar and nicotine."
